claim: Animals and humans replay neural patterns encoding trajectories through their environment, both whilst they solve decision-making tasks and during rest.
source: Animals and humans replay neural patterns encoding trajectories through their environment, both whilst they solve decision-making tasks and during rest.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the broader literature context of the manuscript.

claim: Both on-task and off-task replay are believed to contribute to flexible decision making.
source: Both on-task and off-task replay are believed to contribute to flexible decision making, though how their relative contributions differ remains unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects established theoretical perspectives in the field.

claim: The more flexible a subject, the more they replayed trajectories during task performance.
source: The more flexible a subject, the more they replayed trajectories during task performance, and this replay was coupled with re-planning of the encoded trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between flexibility index and on-task sequenceness.

claim: On-task replay was coupled with re-planning of the encoded trajectories.
source: The more flexible a subject, the more they replayed trajectories during task performance, and this replay was coupled with re-planning of the encoded trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that sequenceness was associated with subsequent policy changes.

claim: The less flexible a subject, the more they replayed previously preferred trajectories during rest periods between task epochs.
source: The less flexible a subject, the more they replayed previously preferred trajectories during rest periods between task epochs.
evidence: This is supported by the negative correlation between flexibility index and off-task sequenceness shown in Figure 4.

claim: Online and offline replay both participate in planning but support distinct decision strategies.
source: The data suggest that online and offline replay both participate in planning but support distinct decision strategies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential correlations of on-task and off-task replay with flexibility measures.

claim: Replay of experienced and expected state transitions during a task is particularly well suited to mediate on-the-fly planning.
source: Replay of experienced and expected state transitions during a task, either immediately before choice or following outcome feedback, is particularly well suited to mediate on-the-fly planning, where choices are evaluated based on the states to which they lead (this is known as model-based planning).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on established concepts in the field.

claim: Off-task replay might serve a complementary role of consolidating a model of a state space.
source: Off-task replay might serve a complementary role of consolidating a model of a state space, which specifies how each state can be reached from other states as well as the values of each state.
evidence: This is a theoretical perspective discussed in the introduction.

claim: Off-task replay directly participates in planning by calculating and storing a model-free decision policy.
source: However, an alternative possibility is that off-task replay also directly participates in planning, by calculating and storing a (so-called model-free) decision policy that specifies in advance what to do in each state (Gershman et al., 2014; Mattar and Daw, 2018; Momennejad et al., 2018; Sutton, 1991).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A pre-formulated policy is inherently less flexible than a policy that is constructed on the fly.
source: Such a pre-formulated policy is inherently less flexible than a policy that is constructed on the fly, but at the same time it decreases a need for subsequent online planning when time itself might be limited.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of different planning strategies.

claim: Online replay promotes on-the-fly (model-based) flexibility.
source: In other words, online replay promotes on-the-fly (model-based) flexibility, whereas offline replay establishes a stable (model-free) policy.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that is tested in the study.

claim: Offline replay establishes a stable (model-free) policy.
source: In other words, online replay promotes on-the-fly (model-based) flexibility, whereas offline replay establishes a stable (model-free) policy.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that is tested in the study.

claim: Recent advances in magnetoencephalography (MEG) analysis have made it possible to study replay in human subjects in relation to learning and decision-making behaviour.
source: However, recent advances in magnetoencephalography (MEG) analysis have made it possible to study replay in human subjects in relation to learning and decision-making behaviour (Eldar et al., 2018; Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological work.

claim: Subjects started each trial at a random state and had to choose a movement direction in order to collect reward from subsequent states.
source: Subjects started each trial at a random state and had to choose a movement direction in order to collect reward from subsequent states (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Subjects learnt beforehand how much reward was associated with each state.
source: Subjects learnt beforehand how much reward was associated with each state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but they did not know initially where states were in relation to one another.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjects did not know initially where states were in relation to one another.
source: Subjects learnt beforehand how much reward was associated with each state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but they did not know initially where states were in relation to one another.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: After the initial two blocks of trials, the reward associated with each state was changed such that persisting with previously optimal moves would result in below-chance performance.
source: First, after the initial two blocks of trials, we changed the reward associated with each state (Figure 1a; grey numbers) such that persisting with previously optimal moves would result in below-chance performance.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: After two additional blocks of trials, subjects were informed that two specified pairs of states had switched positions.
source: Second, after two additional blocks of trials, we informed subjects that two specified pairs of states had switched positions (Figure 1a; 'switch'), again rendering the previously optimal policy now suboptimal.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: A flexible model-based planner would be capable of re-planning their moves perfectly following each of these instructed changes.
source: A flexible model-based planner would be capable of re-planning their moves perfectly following each of these instructed changes, since such a planner has acquired knowledge as to how each state can be reached.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of model-based planning.

claim: A pure model-free planner would need to learn a new policy from scratch via trial and error each time there is a change.
source: Conversely, a pure model-free planner would need to learn a new policy from scratch via trial and error each time there is a change, since such an agent only possesses a now outdated policy that specifies where to move from each state.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of model-free planning.

claim: There was a decrement in average performance following reward and position changes.
source: Examining how subjects' overall performance altered immediately following these changes revealed a decrement in average performance (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown in the performance data in Figure 1c.

claim: There were substantial individual differences in how subjects adapted to reward and position changes.
source: However, there were substantial individual differences in this regard, with some subjects seamlessly adapting to reward and position changes, and others showing drops in performance to chance levels.
evidence: This is evident from the variability in the data shown in Figure 1c-f.

claim: In 2-move trials, an optimal course of action often required subjects to move first to an initial low-reward state in order to gain access to a high-reward state with their second move.
source: In 2-move trials, subjects were rewarded for both states they visited, and thus, an optimal course of action often required subjects to move first to an initial low-reward state in order to gain access to a high-reward state with their second move.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: Individual index of flexibility (IF) was defined as the difference between the proportion of moves that were optimal given the actual number of allotted moves and the proportion of moves that would have been optimal given a different number of allotted moves.
source: Thus, we defined an individual index (IF) of decision flexibility as the difference between the proportion of moves that were optimal given the actual number of allotted moves and the proportion of moves that would have been optimal given a different number of allotted moves (i.e., had 1-move trials instead involved two moves and 2-move trials involved one move).
evidence: This defines the key behavioral measure used in the study.

claim: Subjects adjusted their choices advantageously to the number of allotted moves (+0.21, SEM 0.05, p < 0.001).
source: The results indicate subjects adjusted their choices advantageously to the number of allotted moves (+0.21, SEM 0.05, p < 0.001, Bootstrap test), though there was evidence again of substantial individual differences (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Having a cognitive model that specifies how states are spatially organised makes it possible to plan several steps into the future.
source: Having a cognitive model that specifies how states are spatially organised makes it possible to plan several steps into the future.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the capabilities afforded by model-based planning.

claim: Subjects performed above chance on blind second moves (proportion of optimal choices: 0.56, SEM 0.03; chance = 0.45; p<0.001).
source: We found that subjects performed above chance on these blind second moves (proportion of optimal choices: 0.56, SEM 0.03; chance = 0.45; p<0.001, Bootstrap test), and this was the case even immediately following position and reward changes, when subjects could not have relied on previously tested 2-move sequences (0.52, SEM 0.03; p=0.01, Bootstrap test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Subjects performed above chance on blind second moves even immediately following position and reward changes (0.52, SEM 0.03; p=0.01).
source: We found that subjects performed above chance on these blind second moves (proportion of optimal choices: 0.56, SEM 0.03; chance = 0.45; p<0.001, Bootstrap test), and this was the case even immediately following position and reward changes, when subjects could not have relied on previously tested 2-move sequences (0.52, SEM 0.03; p=0.01, Bootstrap test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Blind-move success was correlated with IF.
source: Most importantly, such blind-move success was correlated with IF (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: More flexible subjects were better able to plan two steps into the future when required.
source: This result indicates that more flexible subjects were better able to plan two steps into the future when required.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between IF and blind-move success.

claim: Chosen moves became gradually more evident over the course of the trial, their decodability peaking 140 ms before a choice was made.
source: Validating the decoder on MEG data from the main task showed that chosen moves became gradually more evident over the course of the trial, their decodability peaking 140 ms before a choice was made (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is shown in the MEG decoding analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Neural and behavioural evidence concur with the notion that flexibility was associated with planning second moves prospectively.
source: Thus, neural and behavioural evidence concur with the notion that flexibility was associated with planning second moves prospectively.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the convergence of MEG and behavioral results.

claim: A hybrid of MF and MB algorithms outperformed substantially either of them alone (BIC: MF = 40821, MB = 43249, MF-MB hybrid = 39908).
source: We found that a hybrid of MF and MB algorithms outperformed substantially either of them alone (Bayesian Information Criterion [Bishop, 2006]: MF = 40821, MB = 43249, MF-MB hybrid = 39908), suggesting that subjects employed a mix of model-free and model-based planning strategies.
evidence: This is a model comparison result based on BIC values.

claim: Subjects employed a mix of model-free and model-based planning strategies.
source: We found that a hybrid of MF and MB algorithms outperformed substantially either of them alone (Bayesian Information Criterion [Bishop, 2006]: MF = 40821, MB = 43249, MF-MB hybrid = 39908), suggesting that subjects employed a mix of model-free and model-based planning strategies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: 84% of inter-individual variance in IF was explained by three parameters that control a balance between model-based and model-free planning.
source: When we examined each subject's best-fitting parameter values, to determine which of these covaried with IF, we found 84% of inter-individual variance in IF was explained by three parameters that control a balance between model-based and model-free planning (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the parameter analysis.

claim: Less flexible subjects had comparable learning rates and a higher model-free inverse temperature parameter (in 2-move trials).
source: Importantly, less flexible subjects had comparable learning rates and a higher model-free inverse temperature parameter (in 2-move trials), indicating that lower flexibility did not reflect a non-specific impairment, but rather, it was associated with enhanced deployment of a model-free algorithm.
evidence: This is a result from the parameter analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claim: Lower flexibility was associated with enhanced deployment of a model-free algorithm.
source: Importantly, less flexible subjects had comparable learning rates and a higher model-free inverse temperature parameter (in 2-move trials), indicating that lower flexibility did not reflect a non-specific impairment, but rather, it was associated with enhanced deployment of a model-free algorithm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the parameter analysis.

claim: The index of flexibility specifically reflected the influence of model-based, as compared to model-free, planning.
source: Thus, our index of flexibility specifically reflected the influence of model-based, as compared to model-free, planning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: There was no evidence of prospective representation of outcome states (images) to which subjects will transition at choice.
source: Applying these decoders to MEG signals from the main task, we found no evidence of prospective representation of outcome states (images) to which subjects will transition at choice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a result from the MEG decoding analysis.

claim: Significant sequenceness encoding the last experienced state transition was found from 50 to 330 ms and from 820 to 950 ms following outcome onset.
source: We found significant sequenceness encoding the last experienced state transition (from 50 to 330 ms and from 820 to 950 ms following outcome onset; Figure 3a; note that the median split is for display purposes alone; actual analyses depended on the continuous flexibility index) and, at the conclusion of 2-move trials, also the penultimate transition (from 130 ms before to 350 ms following outcome onset; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sequenceness analysis.

claim: At the conclusion of 2-move trials, the penultimate transition was replayed from 130 ms before to 350 ms following outcome onset.
source: We found significant sequenceness encoding the last experienced state transition (from 50 to 330 ms and from 820 to 950 ms following outcome onset; Figure 3a; note that the median split is for display purposes alone; actual analyses depended on the continuous flexibility index) and, at the conclusion of 2-move trials, also the penultimate transition (from 130 ms before to 350 ms following outcome onset; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the sequenceness analysis.

claim: Sequences were accelerated in time, with an estimated lag of 130 ms between the images.
source: These sequences were accelerated in time, with an estimated lag of 130 ms between the images, and were encoded in a 'forward' direction corresponding to the order actually visited.
evidence: This is a result from the sequenceness analysis.

claim: Sequences were encoded in a 'forward' direction corresponding to the order actually visited.
source: These sequences were accelerated in time, with an estimated lag of 130 ms between the images, and were encoded in a 'forward' direction corresponding to the order actually visited.
evidence: This is a result from the sequenceness analysis.

claim: Later in the post-outcome epoch, the penultimate transition was also replayed backwards (from 440 to 940 ms following outcome onset).
source: Moreover, later in the post-outcome epoch, the penultimate transition was also replayed backwards (from 440 to 940 ms following outcome onset).
evidence: This is a result from the sequenceness analysis.

claim: Sequenceness was predominantly evident following surprising outcomes in subjects with high index of flexibility.
source: Thus, sequenceness was predominantly evident following surprising outcomes in subjects with high index of flexibility.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical results from the sequenceness analysis.

claim: On-task replay is consistent with contributing to post-outcome model-based planning.
source: This result is consistent with online replay contributing to post-outcome model-based planning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between sequenceness and flexibility.

claim: Moves after which high forward sequenceness was evident corresponded to moves that were less likely to be re-chosen subsequently.
source: We found that moves after which high forward sequenceness was evident corresponded to moves that were less likely to be re-chosen subsequently (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis relating sequenceness to subsequent behavior.

claim: Evidence of online replay for a chosen trajectory was coupled with advantageous re-evaluation of one's choice.
source: Thus, we found evidence of online replay for a chosen trajectory was coupled with advantageous re-evaluation of one's choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the relationship between sequenceness and policy changes.

claim: Off-task sequenceness correlated negatively with IF.
source: Most importantly, off-task sequenceness correlated negatively with IF (Figure 4).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The association of sequenceness during rest with low flexibility is consistent with a proposed role for offline replay in establishing model-free policies.
source: This association of sequenceness during rest with low flexibility is consistent with a proposed role for offline replay in establishing model-free policies (Gershman et al., 2014; Mattar and Daw, 2018; Momennejad et al., 2018; Sutton, 1991).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between off-task sequenceness and flexibility, supported by theoretical citations.

claim: Replay of subsequently chosen moves indicates subjects utilised a model of the task to re-plan their moves offline.
source: This replay of subsequently chosen moves indicates subjects utilised a model of the task to re-plan their moves offline (Momennejad et al., 2018; Gershman et al., 2014; Mattar and Daw, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding of prospective replay, supported by theoretical citations.

claim: Re-planning in light of the new reward associations, before subjects experienced them in practice, requires a model that specifies how to navigate from one state to another.
source: Our reasoning here is that re-planning in light of the new reward associations, before subjects experienced them in practice, requires a model that specifies how to navigate from one state to another.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for prospective planning.

claim: The lack of a flexibility enhancement associated with prospective offline replay might indicate that offline planning is ill-suited for enhancing trial-to-trial flexibility.
source: On the other hand, the lack of a flexibility enhancement associated with prospective offline replay might indicate that, as might be expected, offline planning is ill-suited for enhancing trial-to-trial flexibility.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: There are substantial differences in the behaviour of individual subjects in the sequential decision-making task that corresponds to a distinction in the nature and apparent effects of MEG-recorded on- and off-task replay of state trajectories.
source: We find substantial differences in the behaviour of individual subjects in a simple state-based sequential decision-making task that corresponds also to a distinction in the nature, and apparent effects, of MEG-recorded on- and off-task replay of state trajectories (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The findings fit comfortably with an evolving literature that addresses human replay and preplay.
source: The findings fit comfortably with an evolving literature that addresses human replay and preplay (Eldar et al., 2018; Kurth-Nelson et al., 2015; Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Schuck and Niv, 2019).
evidence: This contextualizes the findings within the existing literature.

claim: Popular tasks for investigating the model-based/model-free distinction have been criticised for offering a better grasp on model-based compared to model-free reasoning processes.
source: However, popular tasks for investigating this distinction (Daw et al., 2011; Decker et al., 2016; Gillan et al., 2017; Gläscher et al., 2010) have been criticised for offering a better grasp on model-based compared to model-free reasoning processes (Gillan et al., 2015; da Silva and Hare, 2019); for rewarding model-based reasoning indifferently (Kool et al., 2016); and for admitting complex model-free strategies that can masquerade as being model-based (Akam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of criticisms from the literature.

claim: The task effectively incentivises flexible model-based reasoning, as this type of reasoning alone allows collection of substantial additional reward (93%) compared to the most successful MF algorithm (80%).
source: Furthermore, the task effectively incentivises flexible model-based reasoning, as this type of reasoning alone allows collection of substantial additional reward (93%) compared to our most successful MF algorithm (80%).
evidence: This is a result from the modeling analysis.

claim: A recent normative model of replay suggests forward replay should prioritise trajectories on which the agent might soon re-embark.
source: In particular, a recent normative model of replay, which aims to account for both online and offline events, suggests forward replay should prioritise trajectories on which the agent might soon re-embark, and backward replay should prioritise trajectories for which one's policy can be improved (Mattar and Daw, 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the cited work.

claim: A recent normative model of replay suggests backward replay should prioritise trajectories for which one's policy can be improved.
source: In particular, a recent normative model of replay, which aims to account for both online and offline events, suggests forward replay should prioritise trajectories on which the agent might soon re-embark, and backward replay should prioritise trajectories for which one's policy can be improved (Mattar and Daw, 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the cited work.

claim: The results are broadly consistent with the normative perspective on replay, showing that evidence of forward replay prioritises frequently chosen trajectories.
source: Our results are broadly consistent with this normative perspective, showing that evidence of forward replay prioritises frequently chosen trajectories, whereas evidence of forward and backward replay follows new observations that can inform one's policy, and indeed predicts appropriate changes in policy.
evidence: This is a summary of how the results relate to theory.

claim: Evidence of forward and backward replay follows new observations that can inform one's policy and predicts appropriate changes in policy.
source: Our results are broadly consistent with this normative perspective, showing that evidence of forward replay prioritises frequently chosen trajectories, whereas evidence of forward and backward replay follows new observations that can inform one's policy, and indeed predicts appropriate changes in policy.
evidence: This is a summary of how the results relate to theory.

claim: The study primarily finds forward sequenceness following outcomes.
source: First, we primarily find forward sequenceness following outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Rather than preplay immediately prior to choice, evidence of on-task replay was found following feedback alone.
source: Second, rather than preplay immediately prior to choice, we found evidence of on-task replay following feedback alone.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Upon observing an outcome, subjects might immediately decide what moves to make next time they start from the same state.
source: However, this result might also indicate that upon observing an outcome, subjects immediately decided what moves to make next time they start from the same state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: More model-based subjects tended to replay trajectories during learning, predominantly reflecting choices they were likely to reconsider.
source: More model-based subjects tended to replay trajectories during learning, predominantly reflecting choices they were likely to reconsider.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The decodeable replay of more model-free subjects reinstated previously experienced trajectories during rest periods.
source: By contrast, the decodeable replay of more model-free subjects reinstated previously experienced trajectories during rest periods, when DYNA-like mechanisms (Sutton, 1991) are hypothesised to compile information about the environment to create an effective model-free policy.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The replay of state-to-state transitions suggests that despite a general inability to draw a map accurately, model-free subjects do have implicit access to some form of model.
source: This replay of state-to-state transitions suggests that despite a general inability at the end of the task to draw a map accurately, model-free subjects do have implicit access to some form of model, though likely an incomplete one.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the off-task replay findings.

claim: The lack of association between offline replay and ultimate winnings indicates that generating a policy offline might not be a good strategy for a task that requires trial-to-trial flexibility.
source: In any case, the lack of association here between offline replay and ultimate winnings indicates that generating a policy offline might not be a good strategy for a task that requires trial-to-trial flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results.

claim: 40 human subjects, aged 18–33 years, 25 female, were recruited from a subject pool at University College London.
source: 40 human subjects, aged 18–33 years, 25 female, were recruited from a subject pool at University College London.
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: The sample size was set to roughly double that used in recent magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies on dynamics of neural representations.
source: To allow sufficient statistical power for comparisons between subjects, we set the sample size to roughly double that used in recent magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies on dynamics of neural representations (Hunt et al., 2012; Kurth-Nelson et al., 2015), and in line with our previous study of individual differences using similar measurements (including 'sequenceness'; Eldar et al., 2018).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the sample size.

claim: Subjects received monetary compensation for their time (£20) in addition to a bonus (between £10 and £20) reflecting how many reward points subjects earned in the experiment task.
source: Subjects received monetary compensation for their time (£20) in addition to a bonus (between £10 and £20) reflecting how many reward points subjects earned in the experiment task.
evidence: This describes the compensation structure.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the University of College London local research ethics committee.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the University of College London local research ethics committee, and informed consent was obtained from all subjects.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: Eight images were used that differed in colour, shape, texture and semantic category to ensure robust decoding from MEG.
source: To ensure robust decoding from MEG, we used eight images that differed in colour, shape, texture and semantic category (Hunt et al., 2012; Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the stimulus selection rationale.

claim: MEG was recorded continuously at 600 samples/second using a whole-head 275-channel axial gradiometer system.
source: MEG was recorded continuously at 600 samples/second using a whole-head 275-channel axial gradiometer system (CTF Omega, VSM MedTech, Canada), while subjects sat upright inside the scanner.
evidence: This describes the MEG acquisition parameters.

claim: Data were low-pass filtered with a 20 Hz cutoff frequency using a sixth-order Butterworth IIR filter.
source: Therefore, to remove fast muscle artefacts and slow movement artefacts, we low-pass filtered the data with a 20 Hz cutoff frequency using a sixth-order Butterworth IIR filter, and we baseline-corrected each trial's data by subtracting the mean signal recorded during the 400 ms preceding trial onset.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing steps.

claim: Support vector machines (SVMs) were used to decode images and moves from MEG.
source: We used support vector machines (SVMs) to decode images and moves from MEG.
evidence: This describes the decoding method.

claim: All decoders were trained on MEG data recorded outside of the main state-space task and validated within the task.
source: All decoders were trained on MEG data recorded outside of the main state-space task and validated within the task.
evidence: This describes the decoding procedure.

claim: Sequenceness is computed as the difference between the cross-correlation of two images' decodability time-series with positive and negative time lags.
source: 'Sequenceness' is computed as the difference between the cross-correlation of two images' decodability time-series with positive and negative time lags.
evidence: This defines the sequenceness measure.

claim: Sequenceness detects sequential relationships even between closely correlated (or anti-correlated) time series.
source: By relying on asymmetries in the cross-correlation function, this measure detects sequential relationships even between closely correlated (or anti-correlated) time series, as we have previously demonstrated on simulated time series (Eldar et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes a property of the sequenceness measure, validated in prior work.
